name: Domain-Driven Design and Bounded Contexts
intent: Divide a large domain into bounded contexts, each with its own model and language, and draw aggregate boundaries inside them, so that teams can change their own meaning of a word without breaking the others, and each business rule is enforced where it can be.
scenario: A shop has four teams: sales, shipping, billing and support. All of them say "customer", and all of them read one shared Customer class: sales has a loyalty tier in it, shipping has addresses, billing has a payer and support has a requester. Every change to the class re-runs the tests of all 5 files and 5 teams. The company splits the model into one context per team, with a thin published language and a translation layer. A shortcut reuses Sales' Customer type in the other contexts, and a loyalty change edits 5 files across 4 teams again. A third team splits the model per entity, and the same change edits 7 files.
problem: The same word means different things to different parts of a business: for sales a customer is a segment with a credit limit, for shipping it is a delivery address, for billing it is a legal payer. A single shared model has to hold all of them, so every team edits it and every change re-tests everyone. Domain-driven design answers by drawing bounded contexts: inside each one a word has one meaning and one model, and between contexts the models are connected deliberately, through a context map and a translation layer (an anti-corruption layer) that keeps another context's model from leaking in. Inside a context, aggregates are the unit of consistency: a rule that spans one aggregate can be enforced in one transaction, and a rule that spans two can only be eventually consistent. The traps are the model sharing that comes back through convenient reuse of types, contexts cut so small that normal changes span several of them, and aggregates drawn too big (contention) or too small (rules lost). Practitioners disagree about how much of the tactical vocabulary is worth using; the strategic part, finding the boundaries, is where most of the value is.

howItWorks.title: Find the words that mean different things
howItWorks.text: Talk to the people who use the system and list the terms they share. Where a word has two meanings (a customer is a payer to billing and an address to shipping), that is a sign of a boundary. The language the people use in one area is called the ubiquitous language of that area, and it should be the language of the code too.

howItWorks.title: Draw a bounded context around each meaning
howItWorks.text: A bounded context is a part of the system, usually owned by one team, inside which the model and the language are consistent. Billing's Customer and Shipping's Customer are two different models that may share only an identifier. The boundary is a boundary of meaning, which is not always the same as a service or a module boundary.

howItWorks.title: Map how the contexts relate
howItWorks.text: A context map says, for each pair of contexts, who is upstream and who is downstream and how they cooperate: a published language everyone translates to, a shared kernel owned jointly, a customer-supplier agreement, or a conformist downstream that accepts the upstream model as it is. Choosing the relationship on purpose is the point, because the default is accidental sharing.

howItWorks.title: Protect a context with a translation layer
howItWorks.text: An anti-corruption layer sits at the edge of a context and translates the other context's model into its own. When the upstream renames a field or splits a concept, only the translation layer changes. Reusing the upstream's types directly saves the layer but makes the downstream conformist, so every upstream change reaches its code.

howItWorks.title: Draw aggregates around the rules that must hold together
howItWorks.text: An aggregate is a cluster of objects changed together through one root, and saved in one transaction. A rule that involves only entities inside one aggregate can be enforced strictly. A rule across aggregates must be handled with events, a process or a compensation, and is consistent eventually. Pick boundaries so the rules that must never be broken are inside one aggregate, and keep aggregates small enough that writers do not queue behind each other.

pros: Each team can change its own model, vocabulary and rules without negotiating a company-wide definition
A translation layer confines the effect of another context's change to one place
Aggregates make clear which rules are strict and which are eventual
The boundaries found are a good basis for module and service boundaries
cons: The same fact is stored and modelled several times, with translation code between the copies
Finding the boundaries takes time with domain experts, and the first cut is often wrong
Rules across aggregates or contexts become eventually consistent and need events or compensation
The tactical vocabulary (entities, value objects, repositories) is overkill for simple data-entry domains
whenToUse: The domain is large, several teams share it, and the same terms mean different things to different teams
A single shared model is slowed down by constant cross-team change and re-testing
You are splitting a system and need to know where the boundaries really are
whenNotToUse: A small domain with one team and one meaning per word, where a single model is simpler
Simple data capture or reporting without business rules, where the strategic and tactical patterns add ceremony
As a way to design service boundaries before talking to the people who know the domain
pitfalls: One shared Customer model for the whole company, so every team edits it and every change re-runs everyone's tests
Contexts that reuse the upstream's types directly to save the translation layer, so a change in Sales still edits Shipping, Billing and Support
One context per entity, so an ordinary change (a loyalty tier) spans 7 files in 4 teams' areas
One big aggregate around everything, which enforces every rule but locks 5 entities for each write and makes writers queue
Aggregates cut so small that a rule like "order total equals its lines" falls between them and can only be eventually true
Calling a context a microservice: a bounded context is a boundary of meaning and may live in one process
Adopting the vocabulary (entities, repositories, factories) without the strategic work of finding the boundaries

quiz.question: Four teams each need something different from "Customer": a loyalty tier, several addresses, a payer, a requester. What does domain-driven design suggest?
options: Keep one canonical Customer class and require every team to agree on each field.
Give every team a bounded context with its own Customer model, linked by an identifier and a translation layer.
Create a separate service for each field of the customer.
Use a generic key-value record so that no team needs to change code.
quiz.explanation: The word has several meanings, so each meaning gets its own context and model. The contexts are connected through a published language and translation, and a change in one team's model no longer has to be agreed and re-tested by all of them.

quiz.question: Shipping, Billing and Support import Sales' Customer type instead of translating it. Sales adds a loyalty tier. What is the likely result?
options: Nothing outside Sales changes, because the contexts are separate.
Only the database changes, because types are not stored.
The three downstream contexts must edit their own code too, because they conform to Sales' model.
The three downstream contexts are protected, because they have their own apps.
quiz.explanation: Reusing the upstream model makes the downstream contexts conformist: its fields and meaning are part of their code. A translation layer would have absorbed the change in one place.

quiz.question: A team draws every entity as its own aggregate. Which rule is then no longer enforceable in a single transaction?
options: A line's quantity stays above zero.
The order total equals the sum of its lines, if Order and Line are separate aggregates.
A name is not empty, if the name is a field of one entity.
quiz.explanation: A transaction covers one aggregate. A rule that needs the order and its lines to change together falls across two aggregates, so it can only be made true eventually, by events or repair. Rules inside one entity are not affected.
